sections.heading: Glossary term: Sidereal Time
sections.body: Sidereal time is a measure of time based on the Earth's rotation relative to distant stars in the night sky. At night, we can see the pattern of stars in the night sky rotate around us. If we pick a star and note when it reaches its highest position in the sky,  then exactly one sidereal day later, namely 23 hours, 56 minutes, and 4.1 seconds later as measured by our clocks, the star will again reach that highest position. This is subtly different from a solar day, which is the time between local noon – defined as when the Sun reaches its highest point in the sky – on two consecutive days. The reason is that the Earth orbits the Sun. For an observer on the Earth, this introduces additional changes of the Sun's position in the sky over the course of one year. During the time it takes for the Earth to rotate once with respect to the distant stars, the Sun has moved and the Earth needs to rotate a little bit more to catch up. That is why a solar day is a little bit longer than a sidereal day. Sidereal time is important for astronomers as it tells them which parts of the sky are overhead at a particular point during the day or night, and thus which objects can be observed. In a standard astronomical coordinate system, the equatorial system, the sidereal time at any place on Earth (excluding the poles) is an angle, namely the right ascension (one of the coordinates used to specify locations in the sky  in that system) of the point in the sky directly overhead. In practice, when observing, present-day astronomers make use of the time measured by highly precise atomic clocks, and then use computers to calculate which clock time corresponds to which sidereal time.

sections.source_html:
Glossary term: Sidereal Time

Description: Sidereal time is a measure of time based on the Earth's rotation relative to distant stars in the night sky. At night, we can see the pattern of stars in the night sky rotate around us. If we pick a star and note when it reaches its highest position in the sky, then exactly one sidereal day later, namely 23 hours, 56 minutes, and 4.1 seconds later as measured by our clocks, the star will again reach that highest position.

This is subtly different from a solar day, which is the time between local noon – defined as when the Sun reaches its highest point in the sky – on two consecutive days. The reason is that the Earth orbits the Sun. For an observer on the Earth, this introduces additional changes of the Sun's position in the sky over the course of one year. During the time it takes for the Earth to rotate once with respect to the distant stars, the Sun has moved and the Earth needs to rotate a little bit more to catch up. That is why a solar day is a little bit longer than a sidereal day.

Sidereal time is important for astronomers as it tells them which parts of the sky are overhead at a particular point during the day or night, and thus which objects can be observed. In a standard astronomical coordinate system, the equatorial system, the sidereal time at any place on Earth (excluding the poles) is an angle, namely the right ascension (one of the coordinates used to specify locations in the sky in that system) of the point in the sky directly overhead. In practice, when observing, present-day astronomers make use of the time measured by highly precise atomic clocks, and then use computers to calculate which clock time corresponds to which sidereal time.

Related Terms:

  • Earth's Rotation
  • Right Ascension (RA)
  • Solar Day


See this term in other languages

Term and definition status: This term and its definition have been approved by a research astronomer and a teacher

The OAE Multilingual Glossary is a project of the IAU Office of Astronomy for Education (OAE) in collaboration with the IAU Office of Astronomy Outreach (OAO). The terms and definitions were chosen, written and reviewed by a collective effort from the OAE, the OAE Centers and Nodes, the OAE National Astronomy Education Coordinators (NAECs) and other volunteers. You can find a full list of credits here. All glossary terms and their definitions are released under a Creative Commons CC BY-4.0 license and should be credited to "IAU OAE".

sections.body_ru: Звёздное время — это мера времени, основанная на вращении Земли относительно далёких звёзд на ночном небе. Ночью мы можем видеть, как узор звёзд на ночном небе вращается вокруг нас. Если выбрать звезду и отметить, когда она достигает своего наивысшего положения на небе, то ровно через одни звёздные сутки, а именно через 23 часа, 56 минут и 4,1 секунды по нашим часам, звезда снова достигнет этого наивысшего положения. Звёздные сутки немного отличаются от солнечных суток — времени между местным полуднем (определяемым как момент, когда Солнце достигает своей наивысшей точки на небе) в два последовательных дня. Причина в том, что Земля обращается вокруг Солнца. Для наблюдателя на Земле это вносит дополнительные изменения положения Солнца на небе в течение одного года. За время, которое требуется Земле, чтобы совершить один оборот относительно далёких звёзд, Солнце перемещается, и Земле нужно повернуться немного больше, чтобы догнать его. Вот почему солнечные сутки немного длиннее звёздных. Звёздное время важно для астрономов, так как оно говорит им, какие части неба находятся над головой в определённый момент дня или ночи и, следовательно, какие объекты можно наблюдать. В стандартной астрономической системе координат — экваториальной системе — звёздное время в любом месте на Земле (за исключением полюсов) представляет собой угол, а именно прямое восхождение (одна из координат, используемых для указания мест на небе в этой системе) точки неба прямо над головой. На практике при наблюдениях современные астрономы используют время, измеряемое высокоточными атомными часами, а затем с помощью компьютеров вычисляют, какое время по часам соответствует какому звёздному времени.
